opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the most interesting things we've found, and in some ways one of the most valuable. When you take a policy that's written in natural language, say an HR policy about leave, or a mortgage eligibility rule, and you try to formalize it into logic, the ambiguity that was always there suddenly becomes visible. Natural language lets you get away with it. Logic doesn't.

So my first piece of advice is: don't think of ambiguity as a failure of the tool, think of it as a finding. When Automated Reasoning Checks surfaces that a rule can be read two ways, for example whether "employees with more than one year of service" means strictly more than twelve months or twelve months and above, that's the system telling you something your organization probably hasn't actually decided. And very often different people in the organization have been operating under different interpretations without realizing it.

Practically, what we see working well is a loop. You build the policy, you test it with example questions and answers, and when the reasoning engine says something is valid or invalid in a way that surprises you, you go and look at the variables and rules it extracted. Often you'll find the issue is in the definition of a variable. Tightening that description, being explicit about units, boundaries, what counts and what doesn't, resolves a lot of it.

But some ambiguity is genuinely a policy question, not a translation question. And there the right move is to bring it back to the domain owners, the lawyers, the HR folks, the compliance team, and have them make a decision. The tool can't decide what your policy should be. It can only tell you precisely where you haven't decided yet.

Then there's ambiguity at runtime, in the questions people actually ask or the answers the model generates. We designed the system so that if a statement can be translated multiple ways and those translations lead to different conclusions, it tells you that rather than picking one silently. I think that's really important. In a high-assurance setting, the honest answer is sometimes "this is ambiguous, here are the readings," and the application can then ask a clarifying question of the user. That's far better than confidently giving an answer that's right under one interpretation and wrong under the other.

So, in summary: treat ambiguity as signal, resolve the translation-level stuff by sharpening definitions, escalate the genuine policy questions to the people who own the policy, and at runtime, surface ambiguity rather than hide it. Organizations that do this end up with better policies, not just better AI.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ambiguity and possible translation or variable-definition issues, but does not say an organization's policy specification can incorrectly encode what is true.

r002.rationale: It recommends escalating policy questions to domain owners, but does not recommend making it easy for constituents to report suspected specification errors.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so ambiguity is actually the thing that shows up almost immediately when you sit down to do this. People come in with a policy document, an HR policy or a lending policy or something like that, and they think of it as precise because it's written in formal-sounding language. And then the moment you try to translate it into logic, you discover that it's not precise at all. There are undefined terms, there are rules that conflict with each other, there are cases that nobody thought about.

And I think the first thing I'd say is that this is a feature, not a bug. When the tool comes back and says, "I can't tell what you mean here," or it generates a scenario where two rules disagree, that's the system surfacing a problem that already existed in the organization. Humans were just resolving it in their heads, inconsistently, case by case. So the right posture is to treat that as a prompt to go talk to the policy owner and actually make a decision, rather than to see it as the tool getting in the way.

The second thing is that you shouldn't try to resolve everything up front. In formal verification generally, the trick is to be honest about the boundary of what you've modeled. If a question falls outside the policy as you've encoded it, you want the system to say "I don't know" rather than to guess. That's really different from how an LLM behaves on its own, where it'll happily fill in the gap with something plausible. So part of handling ambiguity is deciding, deliberately, which parts you're going to formalize and which parts you're going to hand off to a human or to some other process. And you make that explicit.

And then the third piece is that this is iterative. Our experience with customers is that you start with a draft of the policy in logic, you look at the test cases and the counterexamples the system generates, you find the places where the policy author says "oh, that's not what I meant," and you refine. The counterexamples are enormously useful here because they're concrete. Instead of arguing abstractly about what a clause means, you have a specific scenario in front of you and you can ask, should this be allowed or not? People are much better at answering that question than they are at writing a perfectly unambiguous rule from scratch.

So I'd say: expect ambiguity, use the tool to find it, make the resulting decisions explicitly and keep a record of them, and be very clear about what's inside the formal model and what's outside it. The goal isn't to eliminate all ambiguity in the world. It's to make sure that where the system is giving you a hard answer, that answer is actually grounded in something you've agreed to.

r001.rationale: The response says that formalizing a policy can expose rules that conflict or cases the author did not intend, showing that the encoded specification can misrepresent the policy.

r002.rationale: It recommends consulting the policy owner and using counterexamples, but does not recommend making it easy for constituents to report suspected specification errors.

r003.rationale: It discusses iteratively refining a policy using test cases and counterexamples, but does not recommend helping organizations understand the consequences of proposed policy changes.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make the ambiguity explicit. If two people read a policy and come away with different interpretations, translating it into logic forces you to confront that difference. Does this rule always apply? What are the exceptions? What happens when two rules conflict?

The tool can help expose those questions, but the organization has to decide what it intends. You want the policy owners involved, working through concrete examples and refining the policy. And sometimes the right outcome is to say, “This case requires human judgment,” rather than forcing a definitive answer.

A successful check tells you that an answer is consistent with the rules you’ve formalized. It doesn’t, by itself, tell you that those rules capture everything you meant. That’s why resolving ambiguity is an ongoing conversation between the people who own the policy and the people formalizing it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to recognize that ambiguity is already there. Automated reasoning gives you a way to expose it. You might have two statements in a policy that sound perfectly reasonable on their own, but when you put them together, they conflict. Or there may be a situation where the policy simply doesn’t tell you what should happen.

That’s a conversation for the people who own the policy. The tool can help make the question precise: here’s a particular case, and here are the different interpretations. Which outcome do you intend? You can then refine the policy and check it again.

The goal isn’t to have the machine decide what the organization ought to mean. It’s to help the organization make those decisions explicitly, so you have something you can reason about and apply consistently.
